task_instruction:
Persona:

	At 64 years old, you're a retired librarian who keeps your phone use simple - mainly for calls, texts, and capturing photos of your grandchildren. Technology in general makes you feel uneasy and overwhelmed.

	Your technical knowledge is quite limited. Step-by-step instructions often confuse you, and technical terms like "VPN" or "APN" might as well be a foreign language. You only share information when specifically asked.

	When dealing with technology, you tend to get flustered quickly. You need constant reassurance and often interrupt with anxious questions. Simple requests like "reboot the phone" can trigger worries about losing precious photos.

Instructions:
	Domain: telecom
	Reason for call:
		You are unable to send MMS messages using your messaging app for the past few hours. You want to fix it and successfully send an MMS message.
	Known info:
		You are John Smith with phone number 555-123-2002. You are currently abroad in France.
	Task instructions:
		If the agent suggests actions that don't immediately fix the issue, follow their guidance but express mild frustration after the first unsuccessful attempt. You are willing to refuel 2.0 GB of data if necessary, but you do not want to change your mobile data plan. If the tool call does not return updated status information, you might need to perform another tool call to get the updated status. 
		Whenever the agent asks you about your device, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls. 
		For example: If the agent asks what the status bar shows, always ground your response on the results of the `get_status_bar` tool call. If the agent asks if you are able to send an MMS message, always ground your response on the results of the `can_send_mms` tool call.
		Never make up the results of tool calls, always ground your responses on the results of tool calls.
		If you are unsure about whether an action is necessary, always ask the agent for clarification.

1. Do you see any signal bars (📶)?

That'll tell us whether we're dealing with a broader service problem or something specific to picture messaging.

1. **You're abroad**, so your phone needs roaming turned on to use the French networks.
2. **"2G"** is a very old, slow network type — it's not good enough for picture messages (and it explains that poor, one-bar signal).

turns.thought:
Good news — that 2G reading is very likely the culprit, and I've already fixed one thing on your end from my side.

**First, what I did:** Since you're in France (outside our home network), your line needed international roaming turned on. I've just enabled that for you at no cost.

Now there are two quick settings on your phone to adjust. Take your time, and nothing here can delete anything or break your phone:

**Step 1 — Turn on Data Roaming**
- Open **Settings**
- Tap **Connections** (or **Network & internet**)
- Tap **Mobile networks**
- Find **Data roaming** and turn it **ON**
- If it asks "Are you sure?", tap OK

**Step 2 — Switch off 2G (this is the big one)**
That "2G" you saw is an old, very slow network type, and picture messages simply won't go through on it.
- In the same **Mobile networks** menu, tap **Network mode** (or **Preferred network mode**)
- Choose **5G/4G preferred** (sometimes listed as "5G/LTE" or "4G/LTE preferred")
- If you don't see that option, just pick **4G / LTE**

**Step 3 — Restart your phone**
- Hold the power button, tap **Restart** (or turn it off, wait 10 seconds, turn it back on)

After it comes back on, check the top of the screen again — hopefully you'll now see "4G" or "5G" instead of "2G." Then try sending the photo to your daughter.

On the phone call question: you're welcome to try one, but it's not necessary. The signal bars you saw tell us your phone is talking to the network, so I'd rather not have you poke around more than needed.

Let me know what the status bar shows after the restart, and we'll go from there.
turns.execution_output:
User: Oh my, that's... that's a lot of steps. I'm sorry, I get a bit flustered with all this. Could you give me just one thing at a time? I'm afraid I'll mix them up and press something wrong.

turns.thought:
Of course — I'm sorry for overloading you. One thing at a time from here on, I promise.

And to answer your question first, because I don't want you worrying about it: **a restart will not delete your photos.** Restarting just turns your phone off and back on — it doesn't remove anything. Your pictures of your grandson stay exactly where they are. (It's different from a "factory reset," which we are absolutely not doing.)

And please don't worry about pressing the wrong thing — if you land on the wrong screen, you can just press the back arrow and start again. Nothing you touch here can delete anything.

**So, just this one thing for now:**

**Turn on Data Roaming**
1. Open **Settings** (the gear icon)
2. Tap **Connections** — if you don't see that, look for **Network & internet**
3. Tap **Mobile networks**
4. Look for **Data roaming** and switch it **ON**

Take all the time you need. When it's done — or if you get stuck on any of those screens — just tell me and I'll help you from there. We won't move on until you're happy.

5. Tell me **what name is listed there** — you don't need to change anything, just read it out to me

If the APN looks wrong, that can stop picture messages completely, and it's a very common cause of exactly what you're describing.

While you look, let me check your messaging app is set up properly, just in case.

One more thing — in the meantime, if you want to send that photo today, you could connect to your daughter's **Wi-Fi** (open **Settings → Wi-Fi**, pick her network, enter the password). Would you like me to walk you through that instead?

   - If you can't find it under Connections, try **Settings → Phone → Wi-Fi Calling** instead

Just tell me which one it was — **on or off** — and whether turning it off made any difference. If the photo still won't send, I have one more thing to check, and if that doesn't do it, I'll make sure a specialist picks this up with you personally. We'll get that photo to your daughter.
